title: 10500-year-old wooden remains in german lake points to submerged prehistoric settlement
dek: Worked timbers and stone tools lie 20 metres beneath the surface, preserved by waterlogged sediment.
body: About 20 metres under the surface of Lake Arendsee in Saxony-Anhalt, underwater archaeologists have found 10,500-year-old worked timbers, stone tools and animal bones. The discovery came during investigations in spring 2026 by researchers from the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt. Large and small pieces of worked wood, including a wooden post 1.6 metres long showing clear evidence of felling and working, were recovered from the lakebed.

Among the finds are split wooden planks measuring up to 1.3 metres long. Researchers suspect the timbers may have belonged to a constructed feature, potentially even a hut. However, no building plan or other evidence has yet established that the wood formed part of a dwelling. Describing the site as a permanent settlement remains premature. The finds demonstrate that Mesolithic people were active at the former lakeshore and were working substantial pieces of timber there, but further investigation is required to determine the nature and duration of that activity.

Around 10,500 years ago, communities in Central Europe relied on hunting, fishing and gathering rather than agriculture. Even if a structure is eventually identified at Arendsee, this would not necessarily indicate permanent occupation. Hunter-gatherer communities could construct substantial features at camps or other locations that were occupied temporarily or revisited seasonally. The importance of the discovery instead lies in the exceptional survival of worked wood from the Mesolithic period.

Evidence for structures from this period is often preserved only indirectly, through features such as postholes and changes in soil colour. The waterlogged environment at Arendsee has preserved the timber itself, including traces of prehistoric woodworking. A salt dome beneath Arendsee has caused sections of the lakebed to gradually submerge, covering archaeological remains along ancient shorelines. Sediment subsequently covered these remains, creating conditions capable of preserving organic material such as wood.

The lake has already produced archaeological discoveries from several periods, including Neolithic fish weirs and medieval watercraft. Researchers are now using underwater technology to investigate the prehistoric landscape in greater detail. A remotely operated underwater vehicle, deployed in collaboration with researchers from the Fraunhofer Institute in Ilmenau, has produced high-resolution sonar imagery of the former shoreline. The survey is helping archaeologists identify areas for future investigation and plan more targeted dives.

Researchers hope to conduct dendrochronological analysis using the surviving tree rings, although dating such ancient wood is challenging because suitable comparative material is scarce. The timbers are also expected to undergo magnetic resonance imaging in Halle to reveal additional information about their internal structure. Further dives will attempt to establish the extent of the archaeological remains and determine whether the individual pieces of worked wood were connected. For now, the evidence supports the presence of Mesolithic people at the ancient lakeshore, but not yet the existence of a permanent settlement.
Determining whether the timbers belonged to a hut, another type of structure or separate activities will be one of the central questions of future research at Lake Arendsee.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet show whether the timbers formed part of a permanent dwelling or indicate year-round occupation.
settle: Targeted dives and dendrochronological analysis of the timbers would clarify whether the wood belonged to a structure and the seasonality of occupation.
